issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: 'Risky Behavior' is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which otherwise emphasizes hypervigilance, startle, danger in silence, fragmented/avoided trauma memory, and appraisals of betrayal and injustice after police violence. Those other items describe a fearful, threat-sensitive presentation; endorsing active risk-taking as a core threat item pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported elsewhere in the selected nodes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself
issues.explanation: 'Can't Rely on Self' is a weaker fit than the other appraisals for this trauma/context. The profile is organized around external betrayal/injustice linked to police violence, but this item shifts to global self-distrust without corresponding self-blame, shame, incompetence, or strategy items elsewhere. In combination with the strong betrayal/injustice theme, it creates a less coherent appraisal profile.

vignette:
The event that fractured Ricardo’s world happened on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, during what should have been a routine field visit. He was forty-nine then, a parole officer with seventeen years on the job, known among his colleagues for his steady hand and his refusal to carry a firearm. He believed in the work—believed that the men on his caseload deserved a chance to rebuild, and that his role was to hold the line between accountability and compassion. That afternoon, he was checking on a parolee at a halfway house in a neighborhood he knew well, a block of aging brick buildings where he had walked dozens of times without incident. As he approached the entrance, two officers from a joint task force mistook him for a fugitive. They yelled commands he could not follow fast enough. One of them tackled him from behind, driving his face into the concrete steps. The other knelt on his back, pressing a knee into his spine while he was handcuffed. He heard his own voice, high and strange, saying “I’m a parole officer, I’m a parole officer,” but they kept shouting over him. When they finally checked his badge, the one who had been kneeling on him said, “You should have identified yourself sooner,” and walked away. No apology. No report filed. Ricardo lay on the steps for a long moment afterward, his cheek pressed against the grit, his heart pounding so hard he thought it might tear loose from his chest.

For months afterward, he could not hold the memory still. He would start to replay the moment—the weight on his back, the concrete scraping his cheek, the smell of sweat and asphalt—and then his mind would veer away, as if skidding off a road. He would be left with fragments: the sound of gravel under a boot, the feeling of his own breath trapped in his chest, the sight of a crack in the pavement that looked like a river on a map. The whole thing felt unreal, like a scene from a movie that had somehow swallowed him. He knew it had happened—his body knew, because his ribs still ached when he turned a certain way—but his mind refused to accept it. He told his wife once, “It’s like I’m remembering someone else’s life,” and she had no idea what to say.

The triggers came at him from every direction, but the worst ones were the ones he could not predict. He had always been a calm man, deliberate and slow to react, but now his own heartbeat became a source of terror. If he walked up a flight of stairs and felt his pulse quicken, his throat would close and his vision would narrow, and he would have to stop and grip the railing until the world steadied. He began to avoid stairs altogether. At work, the silence between conversations became unbearable. In the moments when the office fell quiet—between phone calls, between footsteps in the hallway—he would feel a pressure building, a certainty that something terrible was about to happen. He started humming under his breath to fill the quiet, or tapping his pen against his desk, anything to break the stillness. His colleagues noticed. They asked if he was okay. He said he was fine, and he said it so often that his wife started to look at him with a worry he could not meet.

He could not stop scanning. Every time he walked into a room, his eyes moved automatically to the exits, to the hands of the people around him, to the angles where someone might be hiding. He started sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants, and when his wife asked why, he said it was more comfortable. He knew he was lying, and he knew she knew, but the truth felt too humiliating to speak aloud. A sudden noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming, a dropped tray in a cafeteria—would send a jolt through him that left his hands shaking for minutes afterward. He began to dread the small sounds of ordinary life.

The worst part was the betrayal. Ricardo had spent his career inside the system, had believed that the institutions he served would protect him if he ever needed protection. They had not. The officers who hurt him were never disciplined. The department that employed him offered a brief, awkward meeting with a supervisor who said, “These things happen sometimes,” and then the conversation was over. Ricardo was left with a certainty that had calcified into something permanent: what happened to him was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. The people who should have protected him had let him down, and he had no way to make it right. He started to see betrayal everywhere. When a parolee showed up late to a meeting, he felt a spike of rage that was out of proportion to the offense. When a colleague disagreed with him in a case conference, he heard it as a personal attack. He knew he was overreacting, but the feeling was too fast, too physical to override.

His marriage began to fray. He stopped talking about his day when he came home, because the stories he would have to tell—the dismissive supervisor, the parolee who lied, the officer who smirked at him in the hallway—would only make the rage boil up again. He spent more time in the garage, organizing tools he did not need, sitting in the dark of his car with the engine off. His wife asked him to see someone. He said he would think about it. He said that for two years.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a moment in the grocery store. He was standing in the cereal aisle, trying to decide between two boxes, when a teenage boy ran past him, laughing, and bumped his shoulder. Ricardo’s body reacted before his mind caught up. He spun around, his fists clenched, his heart hammering, his vision gone red at the edges. The boy looked at him, startled, and backed away. Ricardo stood there in the fluorescent light, breathing hard, holding a box of Cheerios he could not remember picking up. He put the box down and walked out of the store without buying anything. That night, he told his wife he would make an appointment. He did not say what he was most afraid of: that the next time, he might not stop at clenching his fists. He did not say what he was hoping for, because he was not sure hope was something he still had access to. He just showed up at the clinic, sat down in the chair, and waited for someone to tell him what came next.
